title: South Korea Maps 50% Middle East Crude Exit by 2035; Africa's Refining Buildout Quickens
subhead: As US-Iran talks keep prices volatile and Hormuz traffic stays in single digits, Seoul unveiled a decade-long push to halve its reliance on Gulf crude while Dangote's Kenya refinery moves toward ground-breaking. The diversification race the war triggered is turning into written policy.

sections.heading: Seoul Draws Up a 10-Year Exit From Gulf Oil Dependence
sections.body:
South Korea's industry ministry has drafted a 10-year natural resource security plan to cut its reliance on Middle East crude imports to 50% by 2035, according to Reuters, and to add about 20 million barrels to oil reserves by 2030. Seoul currently sources roughly 70% of its crude from Middle Eastern producers, almost all of it routed through the Strait of Hormuz, and the ministry explicitly cites the chokepoint in the plan.

The plan also targets gas: Middle Eastern producers supplied a fifth of South Korea's gas imports last year, and Seoul wants that below 30% within a decade. The draft frames the change as a 'fundamental shift' in how the country sources imports.
sections.whyItMatters: South Korea was among the first importers to feel the Hormuz shock directly — it imposed a fuel price ceiling in March for the first time in three decades and put driving limits on civil servants. Turning those emergency responses into a codified reserve-stockpiling and diversification policy shows the war hardening long-term import behavior in Asia's top buyers, not just short-term scrambling.

sections.heading: Africa's Refining Race: Dangote's Kenya Project Approaches Ground-Breaking
sections.body:
Kenya breaks ground September 30 on the Dangote-backed East Africa Oil Refinery in Lamu, a project priced at $17 billion by Kenyan officials and $20 billion by Aliko Dangote himself, designed to process 700,000 barrels of crude a day at Lamu's deep-water port and serve Kenya, Uganda, South Sudan, Rwanda, Burundi and DR Congo, OilPrice.com reports.

Disclosed financing remains thin — about $1.6 billion against a $17-20 billion price tag, with a $100 million commitment from Tanzanian billionaire Mohammed Dewji and a 30% combined equity offer to East African nations. Dangote is simultaneously advancing two more pipelines — a Djibouti-Ethiopia gas and petroleum line and a $3.5 billion, 2,650-km corridor linking Namibia, Botswana and South Africa — part of a combined continental program he puts at $46-50 billion and ~4,000 km of pipeline. The project faces a rival: Tanzania and Uganda's $20-billion Tanga energy hub with Vitol Bahrain around the East African Crude Oil Pipeline.
sections.whyItMatters: With LNG and crude routes out of the Gulf disrupted, Africa is quietly becoming a competitive theater for regional refining and transit infrastructure. The Lamu and Tanga projects compete for the same Ugandan barrels, and the financing gap (roughly $1.6 billion confirmed against a ~$20 billion build) is the real constraint — big announced plans are outpacing committed capital.

sections.heading: Glencore Joins Project Vault, Routing DRC Cobalt Around Chinese Refining
sections.body:
Glencore committed $500 million to VaultCo, the Export-Import Bank public-private partnership building a critical-minerals stockpile for the US government, Reuters reported. It is the fourth supplier named to Project Vault, after Hartree Partners, Mercuria Americas and Traxys, following EXIM's board approval of a $10-billion direct loan in February plus roughly $2 billion in private capital.

Delivering DRC cobalt directly into VaultCo lets Glencore bypass the Chinese refining capacity that dominates that supply chain's processing. Parallel efforts remain aspirational so far: EGC-EVelution Energy targets up to 40% of US cobalt demand with a 1,775-tonne 2026 quota, and Virtus Minerals is acquiring Chemaf with roughly 20,000 tonnes of annual capacity in mind.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the US critical-minerals industrial policy hardening into named commercial commitments — real money ($500 million) rather than targets. But the article notes none of the direct-sourcing efforts to move DRC cobalt to the US without Chinese refining has yet moved past setting targets, so the headline capital still outpaces physical volumes shipped.

sections.heading: Diesel Squeeze Reaches the White House: Trump Backs an Export Ban
sections.body:
President Trump declared support for a potential ban on diesel exports amid record prices, saying on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, 'I've said let's not send out the diesel... I've called for it,' according to Reuters. The US national average diesel price hit $6.5276 on Tuesday (AAA), and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the administration was weighing whether a ban would be partial or total.

The idea stems from a bill tabled by Rep. Tim Burchett, backed by Senate Majority Leader John Thune; Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum oppose it. Trump has blamed elevated diesel prices on Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian refineries and called on President Zelensky to stop them, while Russia itself has imposed an export ban on its own diesel — deepening a squeeze as Middle East diesel exports are compromised by the US-Iran war.
sections.whyItMatters: A US diesel export ban backed by the president would be a market-reordering move for the world's largest oil producer, and it exposes the contradiction at the center of the war economy: Washington simultaneously wants to keep global supply flowing while facing record domestic fuel prices that make keeping product at home politically attractive. The Treasury/Energy split shows the policy is not settled.

sections.heading: Hormuz Traffic Holds in Single Digits as Saudi Bypass Line Restarts Partially
sections.body:
Only three commodity vessels — including one Panamax tanker — transited the Strait of Hormuz in the past day, preliminary Kpler data cited by Reuters showed, down from four the day before and far below the 10-day average of roughly 15 transits. Tracking excludes ships that switched off their positioning systems to avoid attack, so real, unobserved movement is higher. Bab el-Mandeb traffic appeared steadier at 22 vessels versus a 10-day average near 26, according to Kpler/Reuters.

Meanwhile Saudi Arabia restored partial service on the East-West pipeline — the kingdom's main route to bypass Hormuz and export from the Red Sea port of Yanbu — which had been closed for over 10 days after drone attacks on September 10. OilPrice.com reports Aramco is working to return flows to roughly 4 million barrels per day within a few weeks.
sections.whyItMatters: The Gulf remains effectively closed to observable traffic even as the US-Iran talks revive hopes of reopening. The Saudi bypass restart is the more tangible signal for the market — it eases supply fears now, whereas a diplomatic reopening of Hormuz is still speculative. Asia's crude imports have nonetheless recovered to an expected 23.96 million bpd in September, the highest since the war began (Kpler via Reuters), though still ~13% below pre-war levels.

sections.heading: Briefs: US-Iran Talks Keep Prices on Edge; TotalEnergies Commits to Nigeria Gas
sections.body:
Oil was on track for a sixth straight day of losses as of Wednesday Asian trade, the longest streak since August 2025, with Brent dipping below $100 to about $98.30 and WTI below $90 at $89.49, per OilPrice.com — though prices remain highly volatile around the talks. Trump said US and Iranian representatives 'had a very good meeting... they have another one scheduled in the very near future.' The G7 foreign ministers separately condemned Houthi strikes on Saudi energy infrastructure and called on Iran to stop arming the Houthis.

Separately, TotalEnergies took a final investment decision on the Ima gas field offshore Nigeria (40% operator with partner AMNI at 60%), slated to supply about one-third of the gas required for the Nigeria LNG Train 7 expansion that lifts capacity from 22 to 30 Mtpa, with production expected in 2028.
sections.whyItMatters: The diplomatic narrative is dominating price action far more than the physical reality of a still-closed Hormuz — a disconnect traders are exploiting via short-covering. And the Nigeria FID shows African gas/LNG supply still attracting Western supermajor capital even amid the Gulf disruption, a counter-current to the LNG tightness.

bottomLine: South Korea's plan to cut Middle East crude reliance to 50% by 2035 — complete with a 20-million-barrel reserve build — is the clearest evidence yet that the Hormuz disruption is hardening into long-term policy across Asia's top importers, not just emergency response. While US-Iran talks at the UN keep oil prices swinging (a sixth straight down day midweek despite single-digit Hormuz transits), the concrete moves are in diversification: Africa's rival refinery and pipeline projects, the US stockpiling DRC cobalt around Chinese processing, and Washington debating a diesel export ban under record pump prices. The diplomatic path and the physical supply path remain out of sync, and that gap is where the market's volatility lives.
sources: OilPrice.com, Reuters, Anadolu Agency, Kpler via Reuters, KCM Trade (Tim Waterer), ING (Warren Patterson, Ewa Manthey), Bloomberg, Goldman Sachs, AAA, Kenya officials/Aliko Dangote via OilPrice.com, TotalEnergies
